definition: A high stone or cast-iron bridge carrying a water-filled canal safely across a deep river valley, such as Pontcysyllte.
A safe public record office where historic maps, censuses, parish books, school logbooks, and photographs are preserved.
A horizontal bar and upward broad arrow carved into stone or brick walls by Ordnance Survey map-makers to mark exact height above sea level.
A round ceramic wall sign placed on a British building to honour a famous person or historic event linked to that exact spot.
A smaller local railway line built in the Victorian era to connect market towns and country villages to main city stations.
A water-filled chamber with heavy wooden gates that lifts or lowers narrowboats step by step up and down hills.
The Latin word for a walled Roman army fort, surviving today inside British town names ending in -chester, -caster, or -cester.
An official count of every household in Britain taken every ten years since 1801, listing names, ages, jobs, and birthplaces from 1841.
The organisation founded by Sir Fabian Ware in 1917 that cares for fallen service personnel beneath equal white Portland stone headstones.
Carefully protecting and repairing historic buildings, monuments, and green spaces so future generations can enjoy them.
A carved stone block set above a doorway or high on a gable showing the exact year a house, school, or hall was built.
15 February 1971, when Britain swapped old pounds, shillings, and twelve-penny coins for modern 100-new-pence pounds.
King William I’s great 1086 survey recording over 13,000 English settlements, farms, watermills, and landowners.
A local Census officer who walked from door to door every ten years collecting household forms and copying them into neat books.
A faded hand-painted Victorian or Edwardian shop advertisement still faintly visible high on an old brick wall.
A mapped walking route linking historic buildings, plaques, and landmarks to tell the story of a neighbourhood.
An overhanging upper floor on a Tudor timber-framed house that juts out above the narrow street below to create extra room upstairs.
A historic British building protected by law since 1947 so owners cannot demolish or alter it without special permission.
A round bronze First World War medallion nicknamed the Dead Man’s Penny sent to the family of every fallen British service person.
A carved roadside stone or cast-iron post set along a turnpike road showing travellers the exact miles to nearby towns.
The conservation charity co-founded by Octavia Hill in 1895 to safeguard historic buildings, coastlines, and open countryside.
Recording and preserving older people’s spoken memories about everyday life, work, and local change within living memory.
Britain’s national mapping agency, founded in 1791, whose detailed nineteenth-century maps show vanished mills, fields, and streets.
A church record book introduced in 1538 recording local baptisms, marriages, and burials long before the modern Census began.
A monarch’s official initials stamped onto British postboxes and street furniture, such as V.R., G.R., E.IIR, or C.IIIR.
A tall symmetrical Georgian or Victorian window made of wooden frames of glass panes that slide smoothly up and down on cords.
A weekly handwritten diary kept by British headteachers from 1862 recording attendance, weather, harvests, and inspections.
A concrete hilltop triangulation pillar built by Ordnance Survey surveyors from 1936 to sight exact angles across Britain.
